lead: An alternator is a three-phase AC generator bolted to the engine and driven by a belt. A field winding on the rotor creates a rotating magnetic field; this field induces AC in three stationary stator windings. A diode bridge rectifies that AC into the DC bus that charges the battery and runs the loads. The idea exists because a rotating winding cannot carry the full output current through sliding contacts, while a small field current can. Most petrol and diesel cars use this machine to generate electrical energy while the engine runs.
prereq: You need: the DC bus idea from Chapter 1.6, plus basic three-phase AC and diode rectification.

blocks.text: The physical principle is Faraday's law. A changing magnetic flux through a coil induces a voltage in that coil. In an alternator the rotor carries a field winding. Direct current in this winding makes an electromagnet. The engine turns the rotor, so the magnetic flux sweeps past the three stator windings. Each stator winding sees a changing flux and produces an alternating voltage. The three windings are placed 120 electrical degrees apart, so their voltages form a balanced three-phase set. The stator is the stationary part. The rotor is the rotating part. The field current is small, so it can be fed through slip rings and brushes without heavy sparking. The output current stays in stationary stator windings and goes straight to the rectifier.

blocks.where: e is the instantaneous induced voltage in volts (V); N is the number of turns; Φ is the magnetic flux in webers (Wb); t is time in seconds (s). The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced voltage drives a current whose own magnetic field opposes the change of flux that caused it, which is why the belt must do work to turn a loaded alternator.

blocks.text: The frequency depends on pole count and speed. One mechanical revolution produces p/2 electrical cycles, where p is the number of rotor poles. With speed N in revolutions per minute, the stator frequency is f = (p × N) ÷ 120. Here f is in hertz (Hz), p is the number of poles, and N is alternator speed in rpm. A 12-pole alternator at 6000 rpm gives 600 Hz, as the worked example shows.

The rotor is usually a claw-pole type. One field coil sits on the shaft. Two claw-shaped steel shells interlock around it and form many North and South poles. This shape gives a strong field with a simple, cheap rotor. Two slip rings and two brushes bring in the field current. The stator is a laminated iron core with three windings in slots. Laminated steel reduces eddy-current loss. A fan on the rotor and a vented housing remove heat. The pulley is sized to spin the alternator faster than the engine.

Alternator versions. The common car version is the compact claw-pole alternator with two internal fans and the regulator and rectifier built in. Liquid-cooled alternators sit in the engine coolant circuit and run quieter and suit hot, enclosed engine bays. Brushless (windingless-rotor) versions keep the field coil stationary and use only the claw poles on the rotor, so there are no brushes to wear; they suit commercial vehicles that run very long hours.

items: Rotor: field coil, claw poles, slip rings, brushes.
Stator: three-phase windings in a laminated core.
Rectifier: six power diodes in a three-phase bridge.

blocks.where: V<sub>dc</sub> is the ideal average DC output in volts (V); V<sub>LL</sub> is the line-to-line RMS AC voltage of the stator in volts (V).

blocks.text: The six diodes convert three-phase AC to DC. At any instant the diode pair with the highest and lowest phase voltages conducts. A real bridge drops about 1.4 V to 2 V because two diodes conduct in series. The rectified waveform has six pulses per stator cycle, so its ripple frequency is fr = 6f, where fr is ripple frequency in Hz and f is stator frequency in Hz. The charging circuit around the alternator is in Chapter 1.6.

Manufacturers test an alternator at constant regulated voltage, warm, with full field. The main curve is output current against alternator speed. Below the zero-ampere speed n₀ (also called cut-in speed, often about 1000 rpm) the generated voltage is below the set point, so the alternator delivers nothing. Above it, current rises steeply and then flattens. Four speeds are marked on the curve: n₀; the alternator speed at engine idle, nL (often about 1800 rpm), where the alternator must already supply the continuous loads; the rated speed nN = 6000 rpm, where the rated current IN is quoted; and the maximum permitted speed. The rated current is the current the alternator delivers at 6000 rpm at the stated voltage and temperature.

blocks.where: N<sub>alt</sub> is alternator speed in rpm; N<sub>engine</sub> is engine speed in rpm; D<sub>engine</sub> is crank pulley diameter; D<sub>alt</sub> is alternator pulley diameter, in the same unit.

blocks.text: Why does the curve flatten? The regulator is at full field, so it is not the regulator that stops the rise. The generated emf E grows in proportion to speed, but so does the stator reactance X = 2πfL, because the frequency f rises with speed. The current is roughly I ≈ (E − V) ÷ X; with E = kn and X = cn this gives I ≈ Imax(1 − n₀ ÷ n), which approaches Imax however fast the rotor turns. This self-limiting property protects the alternator from overload. The regulator acts only when the loads need less than the curve can give: it then cuts the field to hold the voltage at the set point, often about 14.2 V for a 12 V system. The pulley ratio is chosen so that engine idle puts the alternator well above n₀; a larger crank pulley or smaller alternator pulley raises Nalt and improves charging at idle. The battery and loads see a DC bus with a small 6f ripple. Losses and voltage regulation are covered in Chapter 1.8.

figure.caption: The worked example's alternator, I = 144(1 − 1000 ÷ n): nothing below 1000 rpm, 72 A at the 2000 rpm idle, 120 A at the rated 6000 rpm, and never more than 144 A, because the stator reactance grows with speed.

examples.question: An alternator has 12 poles and runs at 6000 rpm. Find the frequency of the stator AC before rectification.
steps: List the data: p = 12 poles, N = 6000 rpm.
Use f = (p × N) ÷ 120, because one mechanical revolution gives p/2 electrical cycles and 60 s = 1 min.
examples.answer: The stator frequency before rectification is 600 Hz.
examples.check:
p = 12
N = 6000
f = p * N / 120
print(int(f))

examples.question: An alternator has a zero-ampere speed n₀ = 1000 rpm and a rated current of 120 A at 6000 rpm. Use the self-limiting model I = I<sub>max</sub>(1 − n₀ ÷ n). The pulley ratio is 2.5 and the engine idles at 800 rpm. The loads at night are 70 A. (a) Find I<sub>max</sub>. (b) Find the alternator current at idle and say whether the battery charges or discharges. (c) Find the engine speed at which the alternator covers the 70 A.
steps: At rated speed: 120 = I<sub>max</sub>(1 − 1000 ÷ 6000) = I<sub>max</sub> × 0.8333, so I<sub>max</sub> = 120 ÷ 0.8333 = 144 A.
Alternator speed at idle: N<sub>alt</sub> = 800 × 2.5 = 2000 rpm.
72 A is more than the 70 A load, so 2 A is left for the battery: it charges, but only just.
For exactly 70 A: 70 = 144(1 − 1000 ÷ n), so 1 − 1000 ÷ n = 0.4861, 1000 ÷ n = 0.5139 and n = 1946 rpm at the alternator.
Engine speed = 1946 ÷ 2.5 = 778 rpm. Below this engine speed the battery must help.
examples.answer: I<sub>max</sub> is 144 A; at an 800 rpm idle the alternator turns at 2000 rpm and gives 72 A, so the battery gains only 2 A; the loads are covered down to an engine speed of about 778 rpm.

traps: The alternator generates AC; the diode bridge produces DC. Marks are lost by writing that the alternator generates DC directly.

Output current does not rise forever with speed, and the flat top is not the regulator's doing: the stator reactance grows with speed, so the current self-limits near I<sub>max</sub>. The regulator cuts the field only when the loads need less.
Engine rpm is not alternator rpm. With a pulley ratio, N<sub>alt</sub> = N<sub>engine</sub> × D<sub>engine</sub> ÷ D<sub>alt</sub>; use the alternator value in f = pN/120.
Cut-in speed is not the same as rated speed. Cut-in is where charging starts; rated speed is where rated current is reached.
For a three-phase full-wave bridge, ripple frequency is 6f, not f. Do not use the single-phase 2f result.

quiz.q: Name the two main parts of an alternator that exchange energy through the magnetic field.
quiz.a: The rotor field winding and the three-phase stator winding.

quiz.q: Why does the claw-pole rotor need slip rings and brushes while the stator does not?
quiz.a: Only a small field current is supplied to the rotating field winding; the stator output is stationary and wired directly to the rectifier.

quiz.q: An 8-pole alternator turns at 3000 rpm. Find the stator frequency.
Explain why the output current curve at regulated voltage has a flat top.
quiz.a: At full field the emf rises with speed, but the stator reactance rises in the same proportion, so I ≈ (E − V) ÷ X tends to a fixed value: the alternator limits its own current. Diode and winding ratings set that value.

quiz.q: State the function of the six diodes in the rectifier bridge.
quiz.a: They perform three-phase full-wave rectification, turning stator AC into the DC bus; two diodes conduct in series at each instant.

quiz.q: Engine speed is 900 rpm, crank pulley diameter is 180 mm, alternator pulley diameter is 60 mm. Find alternator rpm and state whether it is above a 1500 rpm cut-in speed.
quiz.a: N<sub>alt</sub> = N<sub>engine</sub> × (D<sub>engine</sub> ÷ D<sub>alt</sub>) = 900 × (180 ÷ 60) = 900 × 3 = 2700 rpm. 2700 rpm is above 1500 rpm, so it is above cut-in.

beyond: Not for the exam. Smart alternators take their set point from the engine ECU over LIN, and 48 V mild hybrids use a belt-driven starter-generator; in electric vehicles a DC-DC converter replaces the alternator. Search for smart alternator and belt-driven starter-generator.
